content: 1. HIV Self-Testing (HIVST) Delivery Methods and Support In the study by Kim (2020), HIVST kits were distributed in health facilities or research units by healthcare workers (HCWs) or researchers. The kits were delivered in person to participants without enhanced instructions, but support included video resources, a study hotline, and confirmatory testing with counseling for those testing positive. Participants were encouraged to report results on an internet-based STI/HIV testing website. Additional materials included pamphlets with routine HIV testing information and local testing venues. Korte (2020) involved secondary distribution of HIVST kits from antenatal care (ANC) clients to their partners. Kits were delivered in person at facilities, communities, or homes without in-person demonstrations or training. Support included advice on partner communication, phone counseling, preand post-test information, and follow-up for those taking kits home. Participants were encouraged to invite their partners to health services for HIV testing. MacGowan (2019) utilized online and mail-based distribution through a website. Kits were mailed to participants without enhanced instructions, but support included phone counseling, mental health counseling, online instructional videos, and remuneration for study activities. Routine HIV testing information was provided on the website. Marwa (2019) also used secondary distribution from ANC clients to partners, with kits delivered in person at facilities, communities, or homes. No in-person demonstrations or training were provided. Support included advice on partner communication, linkage to care and counseling for HIV-positive individuals, and reporting of test use via mobile phones. Follow-up was conducted for all participants, and partners were invited to clinics to learn about their partner’s health and undergo HIV testing. Masters (2016) followed a similar model, with secondary distribution from ANC clients to partners. Kits were delivered in person at facilities, communities, or homes without enhanced instructions. Support included advice on partner negotiation and communication, and partners were invited to health services for HIV testing. Merchant (2018) distributed kits online and by mail through a website or study app. Kits were mailed to participants with no or basic support. Participants were remunerated for survey completion, and routine facility-based HIV testing was encouraged. Nichols (2019) employed community-based distribution by HCWs or researchers. Kits were delivered in person at facilities or communities without in-person demonstrations or training. Support included clinic referral cards or escort to healthcare facilities for those testing positive. Routine facility-based HIV testing was also encouraged. Neuman (2021) used community-based volunteers to distribute kits door-to-door or from distributor homes. Kits were delivered in person without demonstrations or training. Volunteers followed up with clients to check kit usage, collect sealed questionnaires and used kits, and provide advice on referrals for additional care if a reactive result was disclosed. Clients could also drop used kits in locked boxes within the community. Routine facility-based HIV testing was encouraged. Ortblad (2017) involved facility-based and peer distribution of HIVST kits. Kits were delivered in person at facilities, communities, or homes without group demonstrations. Two arms were included: one with HIVST coupons for facility testing and another with kits delivered by peers. Routine facility-based HIV testing was encouraged. Patel (2018) distributed kits in emergency rooms by HCWs or researchers. Kits were delivered in person without enhanced instructions. Results were reported on an internet-based STI/HIV testing recruitment platform. Participants also received routine HIV testing information pamphlets and five referral cards to distribute to peers. Pettifor (2018) distributed kits in health facilities or research units by HCWs or researchers. Kits were delivered in person, and participants were offered a choice between routine testing and HIVST. Women were given five invitations for free testing at local clinics. Routine facility-based HIV testing was encouraged. Tang (2018) used online and mail-based distribution through a social networking mobile phone app. Kits were mailed to participants without enhanced instructions. A crowdsourcing community mobilization initiative was implemented in study cities for intervention design, and additional promotional text messages for HIVST were sent. Routine facility-based HIV testing was encouraged. Wang (2017) distributed kits online and by mail through HCWs or researchers. Kits were mailed to participants without enhanced instructions. Support included online promotional videos with virtual real-time supervision, health promotion videos, remuneration for survey completion, and live chat applications for supervision. Routine facility-based HIV testing was encouraged. Wray (2018) distributed kits online and by mail through a website or study app. Kits were mailed to participants with no or basic support. Monitoring of kit opening was conducted with associated counselor follow-up in one arm. Participants were remunerated for study activities, and letters with routine HIV testing information were provided. 2. HIVST Outcomes and Meta-Analysis Findings A pooled analysis of seven studies showed that 65% of individuals with a reactive HIVST result underwent confirmatory HIV testing. The linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation or HIV care was assessed, with results favoring HIVST over the standard of care in most trials. Adverse events, such as intimate partner violence, were rare. One trial reported four instances of coercion among 13,267 participants, while another reported no instances among 1,063 participants. Certainty of evidence was assessed as low to moderate due to risks of bias, including performance bias (lack of blinding), detection bias (self-reported outcomes), and attrition bias in some trials. Most trials were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, reflecting the region’s generalized HIV epidemic. Outcome definitions varied across trials, ranging from confirmed HIV diagnoses to self-reported reactive results, but results were largely consistent across studies. 3. Study Limitations and Bias Several trials had unclear risks of bias due to insufficient information. Recruitment bias was noted in some cluster-randomized trials. Variability in outcome definitions and small event numbers were observed, which may have influenced the strength of the effect. Despite these limitations, the direction of effect generally favored HIVST over the standard of care.
